MATEO E. DINOPOL Sangguniang Barangay Member Barangay Baganihan Davao City Dear Engr. Dinopol: This has reference to your letter dated 4 November 2024 seeking this Departments legal opinion regarding the authority of barangays in handling land conflicts within ancestral domains, particularly on the following: 1. How can the barangay navigate their authority in the documentation and certification, such as barangay certifications in land conflict matters regarding indigenous people? 2. What is the role of barangays regarding conflicts addressing land conflicts of indigenous people within their jurisdiction? 3. If complaints of indigenous people are filed before the barangay, can the barangay attempt to settle these through Lupong Tagapamayapa? 4. Can the barangay issue a certification allowing constituents to file actions in court? Thus, the request for guidance and legal opinion. Considering the first and second queries being interrelated, we provide one discussion. Attention is invited to Section 1 of Rule IX ofthe Katarungang Pambarangay Rules which states that disputes between members of the same indigenous cultural community shall be settled in accordance with the customs and traditions of that particular community. In connection with this, Section 651 and 662 of RA 8371 (IPRA Law) provides that when disputes involve Indigenous Cultural Communities/lndigenous Peoples customary laws and practices shall be used to resolve the dispute, and that the National Commission on Section 65. Primary of Customary Laws and Practices. - disputes involve ICCs/lPs. customary laws and practices shall be used to resolve the dispute. 2 Section 66. Jurisdiction of the NCIP. - The NCIP, through its regional offices, shall have jurisdiction over all claims and disputes involving rights of ICCs/lPs; Provided, however, That no such dispute shall be brought to the NCIP unless the parties have exhausted all remedies provided under their customary laws. For this purpose. a certification shall be issued by the Council of Elders/Leaders who participated in the attempt to settle the dispute that the same has not been resolved, which certification shall be a condition precedent to the filing Of a petition with the NCIP. Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) shall have jurisdiction over all claims and disputes involving rights of ICCs/lps. Also, Section of the RA 8371 provides that disputes including ownership, control, or rights over ancestral domains or lands fall exclusively under the NCIP's jurisdiction. The barangays may only assist in gathering and submitting relevant documents to the NCIP if requested, and it should refrain from issuing certifications that imply ownership or rights over IP lands. Thus, Barangays must carefully navigate their authority in land conflict matters involving IPs by respecting indigenous customs. adhering to the IPRA Law, and deferring to the NCIP for disputes involving ancestral domains. The barangay's role is primarily to facilitate dialogue, document procedural matters, and coordinate with appropriate authorities while avoiding adjudication or actions that could infringe on indigenous rights especially if the matter includes ancestral domains or lands. As to the third query. we qualify our answer. The general rule is that under Section 412 (c) of RA 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, the customs and traditions of indigenous cultural communities shall be applied in settling disputes between members of the cultural communities. However, if only one of the disputants belongs to another tribal community, the parties must agree upon the indigenous system they would submit themselves to for amicable settlement.4 The only exception here is that the settlement proceedings provided by the katarungang pambarangay rules shall only be applied if the disputants who belong to different tribal community cannot mutually agree on the submission of the dispute with the indigenous system of amicable settlement.5 Thus, the barangay may only attempt to settle indigenous people's conflicts through the Lupong Tagapamayapa if the disputants are from separate tribal communities and cannot agree on which indigenous system of amicable settlement to apply. of that particular cultural community, or where one or more of the parties to the aforesaid dispute belong to the minority and the parties mutually agreed to submit their dispute to the indigenous system of amicable settlement. and there has been no settlement as certified by the datu or tribal leader or elder to the Punong Barangay of place of settlement. However, the barangay cannot issue a certification to file action if the dispute includes ownership, control, or rights over ancestral domains or lands as such matters fall exclusively under the NCIP's jurisdiction, as per Section 52(h) of the RA 8371. This Department is based solely on the facts and representations you have narrated in your letter and our appreciation of the same. We hope to have addressed your concern accordingly. Thank you.
